definitions.meaning: a fairground ride that goes round and round
from the saying that what you lose on the swings you gain on this ride, a balancing gain

explanation.surface: A demand for just and equitable payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' looks like an adjective meaning just, but it is the noun: a funfair ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A merry-go-round is a fairground ride, and the proverb about swings makes it stand for recompense evening out a loss.

clue.text: What parson about to depart on his motor-bike might do?

definitions.text: What parson about to depart on his motor-bike might do?

parts.words: What parson about to depart on his motor-bike might do?
parts.note: a parson is a Reverend, abbreviated Rev, and a biker gets ready to leave by racing the engine

explanation.surface: A vicar prepares to ride off on his motorcycle.
explanation.walkthrough: A clergyman's title is shortened to Rev, so the phrase for gunning an engine also reads as the parson being up and ready.
explanation.definitionFit: To race a motor before moving off is the phrasal verb for raising engine speed.

annotationWithheld.why: Intrude like a novice (7): an anagram of INTRUDE with no word in the clue signalling the anagram (old-style unindicated anagram), so the op has no indicator

clue.text: Panorama' owes its enchantment to this, perhaps

definitions.text: Panorama' owes its enchantment to this, perhaps

parts.words: Panorama' owes its enchantment to this, perhaps
parts.note: alludes to Thomas Campbell's line that it lends enchantment to the view

explanation.surface: Asking what makes a wide view so charming.
explanation.walkthrough: Campbell's 'Pleasures of Hope' says it is remoteness that lends enchantment to the view.
explanation.definitionFit: Remoteness or far-offness softens a landscape, so a view is charming from afar.

parts.note: Under Milk Wood opens on a starless and ...-black night, so the poet's black is a holy book

explanation.surface: A question about the Welsh poet's little book of grudges.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'black book' sounds like a list of enemies; Thomas coined 'bible-black' in Under Milk Wood.
explanation.definitionFit: The scriptures are traditionally bound in black, and Thomas used the holy book as a shade of darkness.

parts.note: the winner of a speaking contest is whoever says the most, split as a verb for speaking plus most

explanation.surface: Asking how far a debating competition can go.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as a verb meaning say plus 'most': in a speech contest the one who speaks most wins.
explanation.definitionFit: Farthest or extreme means the utmost limit, the furthest point possible.

definitions.note: adverb in the clue; the answer is the adjective for heroic narrative verse

indicators.note: only the opening letters of the French shop word are used, its ending dropped

parts.note: the French word for a grocer's shop is épicerie

explanation.surface: A French grocer's shop begins in lyrical style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opens' drops ERIE from EPICERIE, leaving its first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroic narrative verse, such as Homer's, is the grand form of poetry.

definitions.meaning: a sister of the heroine in Thomas Hardy's novel The Hand of Ethelberta
a variety among the pinks, carnations whose petals have a coloured edge

explanation.surface: Ethelberta's sibling is in excellent health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the pink' looks like an idiom for healthy, but pinks are flowers of the carnation family.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy named the girl after a carnation variety with pale petals edged in a darker colour.

parts.note: someone begging with their headgear removed and held out

explanation.surface: Pleading humbly with uncovered head.
explanation.definitionFit: A humble petitioner removes their hat and holds it, so the idiom means respectfully asking.

clue.text: A short last message is very sad

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small or short
PS, postscript, is a message added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A brief closing note can be terribly sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone very sad cries, shedding tears.

clue.text: The Six sit back, under their own vine?

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral six

indicators.note: the word sit is turned to run backwards

explanation.surface: Six people sit back under their own vine, as in the biblical image of peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under their own vine' echoes Micah's 'every man under his vine'; only 'vine' defines, the rest decorates the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the botanical genus name of the grapevine.

clue.text: A portion of " the little children's dower "

definitions.text: A portion of " the little children's dower "

parts.words: A portion of " the little children's dower "
parts.note: Browning's Home-Thoughts, from Abroad calls a yellow meadow flower the little children's dower

explanation.surface: A share of an inheritance meant for young children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'portion' and 'dower' suggest an inheritance, but the quotation is about a wild flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning calls these yellow meadow flowers the children's gift, so one bloom is a portion of it.

parts.note: a raider of ships licensed by a government's letter of marque

explanation.surface: Asking about a sea robber holding an official commission.
explanation.definitionFit: A privately owned armed ship, or its captain, licensed by a state to attack enemy shipping.

clue.text: Step taken daily by Goldsmith's dog-lover to clothe the naked

definitions.text: Step taken daily by Goldsmith's dog-lover to clothe the naked

parts.words: Step taken daily by Goldsmith's dog-lover to clothe the naked
parts.note: Goldsmith's Elegy on the Death of a Mad Dog says the good man clad the naked every day when he dressed himself

explanation.surface: A charitable man in a poem clothes the poor every day.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke in Goldsmith's poem is that the only naked man he clothed was himself, each morning.
explanation.definitionFit: To don garments is the phrasal verb for getting dressed.

clue.text: Indicated with love appreciation of patronage?

annotationWithheld.why: Indicated with love appreciation of patronage? (10): INDICATED + O rearranged with no word in the clue signalling the anagram (old-style unindicated anagram)
annotationWithheld.clue: Indicated with love appreciation of patronage?

clue.text: Tram bound to come to grief in Scotland

indicators.note: a tram that crashes is wrecked, so its letters and the next word's are scrambled

explanation.surface: A tram heading somewhere is destined to crash north of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to come to grief' rearranges TRAM BOUND.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on the Clyde, once capital of the old kingdom of Strathclyde.

parts.note: canny read as can-y, a tool to do with cans

explanation.surface: Praising a clever little device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canny' means shrewd, but here it means having to do with cans.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen tool for cutting the lid off a tin.

definitions.note: adjective in the clue; the answer is a goddess, a divine being

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
RA, Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A man who paints is admired for his heavenly looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looks' is a link here, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The queen of the Olympian gods, wife of Zeus.

definitions.meaning: an Aunt Sally is a target at a fair, so a person open to attack
a lukewarm verdict on a match: it was so-so

explanation.surface: A relative gives a lukewarm remark about a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is a British fairground game of throwing sticks at a dummy's head; hence a target of criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: A legitimate target for attack, and literally a verdict that a contest was middling.

clue.text: "" Well said, old -- ! Canst work i' the earth so fast?" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "" Well said, old -- ! Canst work i' the earth so fast?" (Hamlet)

parts.words: "" Well said, old -- ! Canst work i' the earth so fast?" (Hamlet)
parts.note: Hamlet addresses his father's ghost moving below the stage as a burrowing animal

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet, with the missing word to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 the ghost cries from under the stage and Hamlet likens it to a tunnelling creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A small burrowing animal that digs tunnels underground.

clue.text: Pretty blue, the essayist, after a highball

indicators.note: the essayist's name follows the high hit in the answer

parts.note: a lob is a ball hit high
Elia was the pen name of Charles Lamb, essayist

explanation.surface: An attractive shade, the writer said after a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'highball' looks like the drink but is a high-hit ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden flower with small, often bright blue blooms.

parts.note: signing with just the first letters of one's name to show agreement

explanation.surface: Endorsing something in brief written messages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a few letters' looks like correspondence, but means initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Marked with one's initials to show official consent.

parts.note: Herrick's Corinna, urged to get up and go a-Maying, is a late riser, like the Abraham of a song

explanation.surface: A singer's Abraham is compared with a poet's mistress.
explanation.walkthrough: Herrick's 'Corinna's Going a-Maying' chides her as a 'sweet slug-a-bed' who stays in.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who stays late in bed, a sluggard.

clue.text: *When I have that I may cease to be " (Keats)

definitions.text: *When I have that I may cease to be " (Keats)

parts.words: *When I have that I may cease to be " (Keats)
parts.note: the first line of a Keats sonnet with a missing word, the dread of dying young

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Keats sonnet, with the missing word to supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreads or anxieties, which Keats felt about dying before writing all he could.

parts.note: a town in the Lake District reads as a walk with side attached

explanation.surface: Asking about a pavement in an old English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Ambleside is a Lake District town in the former county of Westmorland; read it as side plus a word for stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: A leisurely stroll, the walk in the town's name.

clue.text: She's only a -- -, as Cob might say!

definitions.text: She's only a -- -, as Cob might say!

parts.words: She's only a -- -, as Cob might say!
parts.note: a cob is a male swan and a pen a female, so his mate is a female swan who is a friend

explanation.surface: A man insists the woman is merely a correspondent.
explanation.walkthrough: Male and female swans are cob and pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A person one writes letters to without meeting, a correspondent.

clue.text: A " must " when there's a Satanic urge

definitions.text: A " must " when there's a Satanic urge

parts.words: A " must " when there's a Satanic urge
parts.note: the proverb says this must happen when the devil drives

explanation.surface: Something obligatory when the devil tempts you.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'needs must when the devil drives' means necessity compels.

clue.text: No game for the Misses Buss and Beale !

definitions.text: No game for the Misses Buss and Beale !

parts.words: No game for the Misses Buss and Beale !
parts.note: a rhyme says the two headmistresses do not feel Cupid's arrows

explanation.surface: A pastime unsuitable for two Victorian headmistresses.
explanation.walkthrough: Frances Buss and Dorothea Beale were Victorian headmistresses; the rhyme runs 'Miss Buss and Miss Beale, Cupid's darts do not feel'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub game of throwing pointed missiles at a board, and Cupid's arrows.

annotationWithheld.why: Clear note suggesting charitableness (9): CLEAR NOTE rearranged with no word in the clue signalling the anagram ('suggesting' is a link), so the op has no indicator

parts.note: Milton's Comus calls the river nymph Sabrina's locks dropping a golden-yellow resin

explanation.surface: Dye falls out of a woman's hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's 'Comus' addresses Sabrina with her 'amber-dropping hair'.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellowish-orange colour, named after fossil resin.

parts.note: crafty read as owning a craft, the ark that held the animals

explanation.surface: A cunning elderly man looking after animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' means cunning, but here it means having a boat: the ark.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical patriarch who kept pairs of every animal on his ark.

parts.note: musical passages marked to get gradually louder

explanation.surface: Things that promote louder noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Gradual increases in loudness in music.
